HAMRAH MECHANIC · INTERNAL TOOLS

A small change. A real-world difference.

Controlled usability tests didn’t explain why inspectors were abandoning a reporting tool. Understanding the environment they worked in led to a much smaller solution than a redesign.

My roleProduct Designer
CollaborationInspectors, support & engineering
Case study publishedJuly 2024
The problemResearchDecisionsOutcomeReflection

The problem

Inspectors used a mobile tool to record vehicle information. Some stopped using it, leaving support teams to handle the information manually.

The visible symptom was low adoption. Before deciding what to redesign, I needed to understand why the experience was breaking down.

Going beyond the test room

I initiated an investigation and ran usability tests, but the controlled setting did not reproduce the difficulty.

I introduced diary research and shadowed an inspector in their normal working environment. Seeing the tool alongside the physical work changed the way I understood the interaction problem.

The lesson was to examine the conditions of use, not just the interface in isolation.

A focused intervention

+16px

More component height and spacing.

We increased the room available for interaction and added missing analytics to observe use after release. The implementation took a few hours.

This was a deliberate choice to make an existing tool more usable without asking the team to rebuild it. I coordinated the investigation and fix with the people involved.

What we observed

In the week after the update, no new usability complaints or rage clicks were recorded. Some senior inspectors returned to the tool.

Follow-up period: one week after release.

The decision that mattered

The key move was changing where I looked for the problem. More polished screens would not have replaced the understanding gained by observing the work itself.

For me, this is practical design: investigate carefully, keep the intervention focused, and check what happens after it ships.
